lessons.title: Know what a row represents

blocks.text: One row, one thing

The customers table has one row per person. The orders table has one row per order. Ada appears once as a customer and twice through customer_id in orders. Repeating a customer reference does not duplicate an order.

queries.label: Customers
queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Use the identifier

A primary key identifies a row uniquely. These tables use id for that purpose. orders.customer_id points to a customer; it can repeat because one customer can place several orders. Switch between Ada and Ben to follow their order references.

queries.label: Ada's orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Ben's orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 2 ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Missing is a separate state

Order 106 has no known amount. SQL represents that missing value as NULL. Recording zero would make a different claim: that the amount is known to be zero. These examples use numbers for amounts and text for names, items and dates.

queries.label: Unknown amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: A customer can have no order

Elm has joined the customers table without placing an order. Compare the two counts. Creating a customer row changes the customer count; it does not create an order. The unit represented by a row determines what a count means.

queries.label: Count customers
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS customer_count FROM customers;

queries.label: Count orders
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders;

lessons.orientation: Identify the thing each table row represents and keep missing values distinct from zero.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Choose the columns you need

blocks.text: Select the useful fields

SELECT chooses the columns in a result. FROM names the input table. Compare all fields with just id and amount: both queries return the six orders, but the second result is two columns wide. The stored orders table stays the same.

queries.label: All fields
queries.sql: SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Id and amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Name the result

AS gives a result column an alias. amount AS price prints the same values under the name price. It does not rename amount in the input table. An alias helps readers understand a report without changing its source.

queries.label: Original name
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Report name
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount AS price FROM orders ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Compute a new column

A SELECT expression can calculate a value for each row. amount * 2 AS doubled multiplies each known amount by two. NULL stays NULL here: an unknown amount does not become a known number because it was multiplied.

queries.label: Original amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Double each amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount * 2 AS doubled FROM orders ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Change the expression

Changing * 2 to + 10 asks a different question. Compare the two expressions for order 102, whose amount is 20. The first scales the amount; the second adds a fixed amount. The alias describes what each result means.

queries.label: Multiply by two
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount * 2 AS doubled FROM orders WHERE id = 102;

queries.label: Add ten
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount + 10 AS increased FROM orders WHERE id = 102;

lessons.orientation: Use SELECT and aliases to shape a result without changing the stored table.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Write the condition you mean

blocks.text: Keep rows that pass

WHERE keeps rows whose condition is true. amount >= 40 keeps 101, 103 and 104; amount >= 80 keeps only the two 80 amounts. The NULL amount does not satisfy either comparison. Increase the threshold and observe which rows leave.

queries.label: At least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: At least 80
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 80 ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Both conditions or either

AND requires both conditions. paid AND amount >= 40 keeps two rows. OR accepts either condition, so paid OR amount >= 40 also includes the smaller paid orders and pending order 104. Parentheses make the intended grouping clear in longer conditions.

queries.label: Both conditions
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Either condition
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' OR amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Decide on the boundaries

BETWEEN 20 AND 40 includes both 20 and 40. The open interval amount > 20 AND amount < 40 includes neither boundary, leaving no rows in this dataset. Inclusive and exclusive comparisons describe different sets.

queries.label: Include 20 and 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount BETWEEN 20 AND 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Exclude 20 and 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 20 AND amount < 40 ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Match a set or a pattern

IN ('Book', 'Lamp') keeps either named item. LIKE 'B%' keeps item names beginning with B; % can stand for zero or more characters. Here that finds the Book orders. Use IS NULL to find a missing amount; amount = NULL does not test missingness.

queries.label: Book or Lamp
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE item IN ('Book', 'Lamp') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Starts with B
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE item LIKE 'B%' ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Missing amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL ORDER BY id;

lessons.orientation: Use SQL conditions to select exactly the rows your question requires.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Make the first row meaningful

blocks.text: Order is an instruction

A table's apparent display order is not a promised query order. ORDER BY id ASC asks for increasing ids; DESC reverses them. Both results contain the same orders. Use an explicit order whenever first, last or next matters.

queries.label: Increasing ids
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id ASC;

queries.label: Decreasing ids
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC;

blocks.text: Break a tie

Two known amounts are 80. ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC puts 101 before 103. Reversing the id tie-breaker puts 103 first. Ordering by amount alone would leave their relative order unspecified. This example filters out the missing amount before sorting.

queries.label: Lower id wins ties
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Higher id wins ties
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id DESC;

blocks.text: Take the top rows

LIMIT caps the number of result rows. With amount descending and id ascending, LIMIT 2 returns the two 80 orders. LIMIT 3 adds the 40 order. A limit without a meaningful order does not establish which records are the largest.

queries.label: Top two
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC LIMIT 2;

queries.label: Top three
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC LIMIT 3;

blocks.text: Filter before selecting the top

WHERE first defines the eligible orders. Sorting the paid orders from smallest amount upward gives 102, 105, 101, 103. LIMIT 2 then keeps the two smallest paid orders. Changing DESC selects the largest paid orders instead.

queries.label: Smallest paid
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY amount ASC, id ASC LIMIT 2;

queries.label: Largest paid
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC LIMIT 2;

lessons.orientation: Use a deterministic order to decide which rows a limited result retains.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Count distinct things

blocks.text: Remove repeated result values
The original orders contain six customer references: 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3. SELECT DISTINCT customer_id removes repeated result rows and leaves three ids. It does not delete orders from the input table.

queries.label: Every reference
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, id;

queries.label: Distinct customers
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id;

blocks.text: The whole selected row matters

DISTINCT compares the full SELECT list. DISTINCT item returns three item names. DISTINCT item, id returns six pairs because every order id is different. Adding a column can stop two rows from being duplicates.

queries.label: Distinct items
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT item FROM orders ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Distinct item and id
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT item, id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: One missing result value

The amount column contains 80, 20, 80, 40, 20 and NULL. DISTINCT amount retains 20, 40, 80 and one NULL result. COUNT(DISTINCT amount) counts only the three known distinct amounts. The two queries answer different counting questions.

queries.label: Distinct amounts
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT amount FROM orders ORDER BY amount;

queries.label: Count known distinct amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

blocks.text: A combination can repeat

In these orders, every Desk and Book is paid, and every Lamp is pending. DISTINCT item, status returns three combinations. DISTINCT customer_id, status returns five: customer 2 and customer 3 each have both statuses.

queries.label: Item and status
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT item, status FROM orders ORDER BY item, status;

queries.label: Customer and status
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, status FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, status;

lessons.orientation: Distinguish result rows, distinct values and distinct combinations of values.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Choose the right denominator

blocks.text: Count rows or known values

COUNT(*) counts all six orders. COUNT(amount) counts the five non-NULL amounts. The difference exposes a missing value. Counting rows is useful for activity; counting a column is useful when you need to know how many observations are known.

queries.label: Count every order
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders;

queries.label: Count known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

blocks.text: Average the known amounts

SUM(amount) is 240. AVG(amount) divides that sum by the five known amounts, giving 48. It does not divide by all six orders. COALESCE(amount, 0) replaces the missing value with zero and changes the resulting average to 40.

queries.label: Keep missing separate
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders;

queries.label: Fill missing with zero
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS total, AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS mean FROM orders;

blocks.text: Minimum and maximum

MIN(amount) and MAX(amount) select the smallest and largest known amounts: 20 and 80. The pending orders contain one known amount, 40, and one NULL. Their minimum and maximum are both 40; that does not mean the missing amount was 40.

queries.label: All orders
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS minimum, MAX(amount) AS maximum FROM orders;

queries.label: Pending only
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS minimum, MAX(amount) AS maximum FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';

blocks.text: No matches still has a meaning

No order has amount greater than 100. An aggregate query without GROUP BY still returns one result row: COUNT(*) is zero, while SUM(amount) and AVG(amount) are NULL. An absent total and a measured zero total are different claims.

queries.label: Known orders
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders;

queries.label: No matches
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders WHERE amount > 100;

lessons.orientation: Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX while keeping missing values visible.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Build a grouped report

blocks.text: One result per group

GROUP BY item puts orders with the same item together. SUM(amount) then adds known amounts inside each group. The result has three rows: Book totals 40, Desk totals 160, and Lamp totals 40. The report's rows now represent items rather than orders.

queries.label: Group by item
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Group by status
queries.sql: SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

blocks.text: Count the data inside a group

Each item has two orders. Lamp has only one known amount, so COUNT(*) is two and COUNT(amount) is one for that group. A grouped report can show both counts next to a total, making incomplete measurements visible.

queries.label: Order counts
queries.sql: SELECT item, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Known amount counts
queries.sql: SELECT item, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

blocks.text: Filter totals with HAVING

HAVING tests a completed group. HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100 keeps only Desk. Raising the threshold to 200 leaves no groups. WHERE cannot replace this group-total test: it operates on individual input rows before the grouping.

queries.label: Total at least 100
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100 ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Total at least 200
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item HAVING SUM(amount) >= 200 ORDER BY item;

blocks.text: Define the eligible rows first

WHERE status = 'paid' removes pending orders before groups are made. The resulting item report contains Book and Desk only. HAVING can then keep groups whose paid total reaches a threshold. Read the row filter and group filter separately.

queries.label: Every status
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Paid total at least 50
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY item HAVING SUM(amount) >= 50 ORDER BY item;

lessons.orientation: Build a report whose rows represent groups, then filter its calculated totals.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Follow a relationship between tables

blocks.text: Bring the name to the order

Orders store customer_id; customers store the person's name. JOIN customers ON customers.id = orders.customer_id pairs each order with its customer. Ada's two orders produce two rows. The result still represents orders, now with names attached.

queries.label: Order references
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Names attached
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, c.name, o.amount FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

blocks.text: The matches set the count

An INNER JOIN retains matching pairs. Dee has no order, so she has no row in this result. Selecting DISTINCT c.name changes the report to customers who ordered, leaving Ada, Ben and Cy. Choose the result's unit before interpreting its count.

queries.label: One row per match
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Customers who ordered
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.name;

blocks.text: A missing condition multiplies rows

CROSS JOIN pairs every customer with every order. Four customers and six orders make 24 pairs. That is useful for some combinations, but it does not mean all those people placed those orders. Compare it with the key-based join.

queries.label: Match the reference
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Every possible pair
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c CROSS JOIN orders AS o ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

blocks.text: Join first, then select the report

A relationship predicate compares the customer's key with the order's customer reference. Comparing customers.id to orders.id is a different condition and finds no matches here. After a correct join, a row filter can keep only paid orders.

queries.label: Paid matched orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Wrong columns
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.id ORDER BY o.id;

lessons.orientation: Join keys deliberately and account for every matching pair.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Keep the customers with no orders

blocks.text: Keep the left-hand row

LEFT JOIN retains every customer. The six order matches remain, and Dee adds one row with NULL order fields. Those NULL fields mean no order matched; they do not describe an order with a missing amount.

queries.label: Only matches
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Keep every customer
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

blocks.text: Count the matched key

After a left join, COUNT(*) includes Dee's retained row and would report one. COUNT(o.id) counts actual matched orders and reports zero for Dee. The order key is present on every matched order, even when its amount is missing.

queries.label: Count joined rows
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS rows FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Count matched orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

blocks.text: A WHERE filter can remove the retained row

WHERE o.status = 'paid' is tested after the join. Dee's NULL status does not pass, so her row disappears. Putting the paid test in ON limits which orders match while still preserving every customer. Compare the two result sets.

queries.label: Paid test in WHERE
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Paid test in ON
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

blocks.text: Find the absence itself

WHERE o.id IS NULL selects customers with no matched order. Here it finds Dee. Testing o.amount IS NULL would also find Cy's actual order 106, whose amount is unknown. Use a guaranteed matched key when you mean no relationship exists.

queries.label: No matching order
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: No known amount
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.amount IS NULL ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

lessons.orientation: Preserve unmatched customers without counting them as orders.
lessons.reviewLabel: Keep the customers with no orders
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Keep unmatched rows on either side

blocks.text: Which side stays?

A new guest order 107 has a NULL customer reference. LEFT JOIN preserves customers, including Dee, but omits that unmatched order. RIGHT JOIN preserves orders, including the guest order, but omits Dee. Both results have seven rows here, yet they represent different records.

queries.label: Preserve customers
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Preserve orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c RIGHT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

blocks.text: Keep both unmatched records

FULL OUTER JOIN retains the six matched orders, Dee's customer-only row and the guest order's order-only row. Its eight rows include both kinds of absence. The matching condition still decides which rows can be paired.

queries.label: Matches only
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c INNER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Preserve both sides
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

blocks.text: Inspect the missing side

In this full join, o.id IS NULL finds Dee's customer-only row. c.id IS NULL finds the guest order, which has no matching customer. Compare the tests. A row count alone cannot tell you which side of a relationship is absent.

queries.label: Customer without order
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Order without customer
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

blocks.text: Restrict matches without hiding the rest

Adding o.status = 'paid' to a full join's ON clause means only paid orders can match a customer. Pending orders 104 and 106 still remain as unmatched order rows, alongside the guest order. FULL preserves both sides even when an ON condition fails.

queries.label: Match every status
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Only paid matches
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid' WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

lessons.orientation: Compare RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN with a guest order that has no customer reference.
lessons.reviewLabel: Keep unmatched rows on either side
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Use one query to define another

blocks.text: Compare with a calculated value

A subquery can supply a value to an outer condition. AVG(amount) returns 48 for the known amounts. The outer query keeps amounts above that value, finding the two 80 orders. Raising a fixed threshold to 80 instead excludes those equal amounts.

queries.label: Above the average
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Strictly above 80
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 80 ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Use a returned set

The customer subquery returns ids in the North region: 1 and 3. IN uses that set to select their orders. A different subquery can select South instead. The outer result remains one row per qualifying order, including an order with a missing amount.

queries.label: North customers' orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'North') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: South customers' orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'South') ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Ask whether a match exists

EXISTS is true if the subquery returns at least one row. This correlated subquery checks orders for each current customer. Ada has two matches, but the outer customers query returns her once. NOT EXISTS finds Dee, who has no orders.

queries.label: At least one order
queries.sql: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers AS c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: No orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers AS c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

blocks.text: Compare with the appropriate group

A correlated average can change with the outer row. Compare each known amount with the average for that same item. Both Desk amounts equal 80 and both Book amounts equal 20; Lamp's only known amount is 40. None is strictly above its own item's average.

queries.label: Above overall average
queries.sql: SELECT id, item, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Above its item average
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, o.item, o.amount FROM orders AS o WHERE o.amount > (SELECT AVG(i.amount) FROM orders AS i WHERE i.item = o.item) ORDER BY o.id;

lessons.orientation: Use scalar subqueries, IN and EXISTS without multiplying the outer result.
lessons.reviewLabel: Use one query to define another
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Combine reports deliberately

blocks.text: Stack results with the same shape

UNION combines compatible SELECT results vertically. The first result lists paid order ids; the second lists ids with amount at least 40. Both select one column. UNION does not attach customer fields to orders as a join would.

queries.label: Paid orders
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Paid or at least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Decide whether duplicates matter

Orders 101 and 103 satisfy both selections. UNION removes repeated result rows and returns five ids. UNION ALL keeps both occurrences and returns seven rows. Repeated results can be useful when occurrences are the thing being counted.

queries.label: Remove repeated rows
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Keep occurrences
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION ALL SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Compare the whole result row

UNION removes duplicates across all selected columns. Adding a label such as 'paid' or 'large' makes the two occurrences of order 101 different rows. A category label changes the comparison even when the underlying id repeats.

queries.label: Id only
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Id and selection label
queries.sql: SELECT id, 'paid' AS selection FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id, 'large' AS selection FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id, selection;

blocks.text: Order the combined result

ORDER BY at the end sorts the combined result. LIMIT at the end caps that combined result. With unique ids increasing, LIMIT 3 keeps 101, 102 and 103. Each SELECT in this example contributes the same number of columns.

queries.label: Combined result
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: First three combined ids
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id LIMIT 3;

lessons.orientation: Stack compatible results with UNION or UNION ALL and account for overlapping rows.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Rank rows without collapsing them

blocks.text: Keep the individual records

GROUP BY amount makes one row for each known amount. A window calculation keeps each known order row and adds a value alongside it. ROW_NUMBER numbers those rows in the specified order; it does not replace them with groups.

queries.label: Collapse into amount groups
queries.sql: SELECT amount, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL GROUP BY amount ORDER BY amount DESC;

queries.label: Keep every known order
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

blocks.text: Equal values share a rank

RANK with ORDER BY amount DESC gives both 80 amounts rank 1. Two rows occupy that first rank, so the next value, 40, has rank 3. The output still lists every order. The final id tie-breaker makes the display order stable without changing the rank definition.

queries.label: Number each row
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Share ranks for equal amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

blocks.text: Choose whether ranks have gaps

DENSE_RANK also gives equal amounts the same rank, but the next distinct amount gets the next integer. The 40 amount has dense rank 2 and ordinary rank 3. Use the definition that matches the meaning of your report.

queries.label: Ranks with gaps
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Ranks without gaps
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

blocks.text: A tie-breaker changes a rank's meaning

RANK orders by all expressions inside OVER. Adding id to that window order makes every order different, so the two 80 amounts no longer tie. Keep id only in the final display order when your ranking is intended to compare amounts alone.

queries.label: Rank the amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Rank amount and id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lessons.orientation: Distinguish ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK and choose tie behaviour deliberately.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Choose which rows a window sees

blocks.text: Start again for each customer

PARTITION BY customer_id creates a separate window for each customer. ROW_NUMBER ordered by id then starts at 1 for each person's first order. Without PARTITION BY, all six orders belong to one window and are numbered together.

queries.label: One global window
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: One window per customer
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Attach a group total

SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY status) places the relevant status total next to every order. Each paid row gets 200; each pending row gets 40 from its one known amount. GROUP BY would instead collapse the report to two status rows.

queries.label: Group the report
queries.sql: SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

queries.label: Keep rows with status totals
queries.sql: SELECT id, status, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY status) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Divide an ordered set into buckets

NTILE(3) distributes the five known-amount orders into three buckets as evenly as possible. Ordered by id, the bucket sizes are two, two and one; larger buckets come first. These buckets divide positions, not distinct amount values.

queries.label: Two buckets
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, NTILE(2) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Three buckets
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Filter after the calculation

To keep each customer's first order, first compute position in an inner query. The outer WHERE position = 1 then filters that result. Filtering input rows before the window calculation would change what the window gets to see.

queries.label: Number all customer orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: First order per customer
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, position FROM (SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders) WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY id;

lessons.orientation: Calculate within each row's group and filter the resulting values.
lessons.reviewLabel: Choose which rows a window sees
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

lessons.title: Read the rows before and after

blocks.text: Extend a running total

SUM(amount) with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW adds known amounts from the first ordered row through the current row. Ordered by id, the totals are 80, 100, 180, 220, 240 and 240. The missing last amount does not add a known value.

queries.label: Known grand total
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER () AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Running known total
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

blocks.text: Peers can enter together

A RANGE frame ordered by day includes the current day's peers. On September 2, both orders 102 and 103 show 180. A ROWS frame ordered by day and id includes records one by one, showing 100 and then 180. The frame describes which records contribute.

queries.label: One row at a time
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY day, id;

queries.label: Include the day's peers
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY day, id;

blocks.text: Look at the previous row

LAG(amount) returns the previous row's amount in the window order. With ids increasing, order 104 sees order 103's amount, 80. The first row has no predecessor, so its LAG is NULL unless a default was supplied. Reversing the order changes the neighbours.

queries.label: Previous in increasing id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ASC) AS previous FROM orders ORDER BY id ASC;

queries.label: Previous in decreasing id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id DESC) AS previous FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC;

blocks.text: Look ahead explicitly

LEAD(amount) returns the next row's amount. In increasing id order, order 103 sees 104's amount, 40. Order 105 sees NULL because the next amount is missing; order 106 sees NULL because no next row exists. The same displayed value can have different causes.

queries.label: Next amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LEAD(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Next id
queries.sql: SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lessons.orientation: Specify running frames and use LAG or LEAD with an explicit ordering.
lessons.reviewLabel: Read the rows before and after
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

questions.prompt: Name the table that has one row per order.
hints: Follow the thing each id identifies.

questions.prompt: How many orders in the original data reference customer_id = 1?
hints: Read customer_id, not the order's id.
Count the rows with customer_id = 1.
Follow customer_id in the order table; orders 101 and 102 belong to Ada.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 101 and 102 reference customer 1; there are two.

questions.prompt: The amount for order 106 is unknown. Which value records that?
hints: Unknown and known to be zero make different claims.

questions.prompt: In the Elm example, how many rows are in customers?
hints: Elm adds one customer row.
Start with four customers and add the new person.
Add Elm to Ada, Ben, Cy and Dee; count the resulting people.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four original customers plus Elm make five customer rows.

questions.prompt: Three customers each place two orders. How many rows should a one-row-per-order table have?
hints: Count orders rather than people.
Multiply the number of people by the orders per person.
Evaluate 3 × 2; each customer contributes two order rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three customers times two orders each makes six order rows.

questions.prompt: Which column can repeat without making an order id ambiguous?
hints: Several orders can refer to the same customer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: orders.customer_id can repeat because one customer can place several orders. The separate order id still identifies each order uniquely.

questions.prompt: How many columns does SELECT id, amount FROM orders return?
hints: Count names in the SELECT list.
Rows and columns measure different things.
The SELECT list is id, amount. Count each listed column once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The SELECT list names id and amount: two columns.

questions.prompt: What does amount AS price change?
hints: An alias belongs to the result.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: AS price labels the column in this query's result. It does not rename the stored amount column.

questions.prompt: Order 101 has amount 80. What is amount * 2?
hints: Apply the expression to the row's amount.
Multiply 80 by two.
Evaluate 80 × 2; AS would only name the result column.

hints: This expression adds a fixed amount.
Add ten to twenty.
Evaluate 20 + 10; multiplication is not part of this expression.

hints: AS names the column; the multiplication produces the value.
Multiply fifteen by three.
Evaluate 15 × 3, keeping the alias separate from the value.

hints: SELECT reads the table; this alias does not alter its schema.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The stored column remains amount. The alias price belongs to the query result, so another query can still refer to amount.

questions.prompt: How many orders satisfy amount >= 40?
hints: Read only known amounts.
Include the boundary amount 40.
Inspect orders 101, 103 and 104; each passes the inclusive threshold.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 101, 103 and 104 satisfy the comparison; 106 has a missing amount.

hints: Each row must satisfy both tests.
Exclude pending 104 and the two smaller paid orders.
Orders 101 and 103 pass both conditions; the other known large order is pending.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only paid orders 101 and 103 also have amount at least 40.

questions.prompt: Which values can pass amount BETWEEN 20 AND 40?
hints: BETWEEN includes its two boundaries.

acceptedIdeas: Values from 20 through 40, including both ends
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: BETWEEN includes both endpoints, so 20 and 40 pass as well as values between them. An unknown amount does not pass this comparison.

questions.prompt: How many orders have item IN ('Book', 'Lamp')?
hints: An item can match either value in the list.
The missing amount does not stop its item from being Lamp.
The Book rows are 102 and 105; the Lamp rows are 104 and 106.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two Book orders and two Lamp orders make four.

questions.prompt: How many orders satisfy amount > 20 AND amount < 80?
hints: Both inequalities are strict.
Count known amounts strictly between the boundaries.
The known amounts are 80, 20, 80, 40 and 20. Keep only strict interior values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only order 104 has amount 40; the 20 and 80 boundaries are excluded.

questions.prompt: Which condition finds an unknown amount?
hints: SQL provides a missing-value predicate.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use amount IS NULL to test for a missing value. Equality to NULL does not evaluate to true in SQL.

questions.prompt: What promises that the result uses increasing order ids?
hints: Ordering must be part of the query.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ORDER BY id ASC explicitly requests increasing ids. Without ORDER BY, the query makes no promise about the order of its result rows.

questions.prompt: With ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC over known amounts, which id appears first?
hints: Compare amounts before ids.
Use increasing id to break the 80 tie.
Among the tied maximum amounts, choose the smaller order id.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The maximum amount is 80; the lower of its two order ids is 101.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the amounts in the top three known orders by amount descending?
hints: Take the three largest known amounts.
Add both 80 amounts and the 40 amount.
Evaluate 80 + 80 + 40 after selecting the three largest known amounts.

questions.prompt: WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY amount ASC, id ASC LIMIT 2 selects which set?
hints: Read the filter, direction and limit together.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: WHERE first keeps paid rows, ORDER BY amount ASC puts the smallest amounts first, and LIMIT 2 keeps the first two. id provides a stable order for ties.

questions.prompt: How many rows can LIMIT 10 return when only four rows satisfy WHERE?
hints: LIMIT is an upper bound.
There are only four eligible rows.
Use the smaller of the eligible-row count and the limit; LIMIT adds no rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A limit does not create records; the result contains the four eligible rows.

questions.prompt: Two rows tie on amount. How do you make their order deterministic?
hints: A unique secondary sort key separates the tied rows.

acceptedIdeas: Add a unique id as a tie-breaker
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Add a unique id after amount in ORDER BY. It settles ties on amount so the same rows have a defined order.

choices.label: Add a unique id as a tie-breaker

questions.prompt: How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders return?
hints: Collect the different customer ids.
Repeated references collapse into one result row.
Collect the set of customer ids before counting it: repeated references do not add new members.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The distinct ids are 1, 2 and 3.

questions.prompt: Why does DISTINCT item, id still return six rows?
hints: DISTINCT compares the entire selected row.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: DISTINCT compares the complete selected row. Even when item repeats, the unique id makes every item-and-id pair different.

questions.prompt: What does COUNT(DISTINCT amount) return for the original orders?
hints: Ignore missing values for this count.
Count different known amounts, not orders.
The known amount set is 20, 40 and 80; count those distinct members.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known distinct amounts are 20, 40 and 80. COUNT does not include NULL.

questions.prompt: How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, status FROM orders return?
hints: List the statuses separately for each customer.
Compare the full two-column row.
List each customer's statuses separately, then count different full pairs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Customer 1 has paid; customer 2 has paid and pending; customer 3 has paid and pending. That makes five pairs.

questions.prompt: A result column contains North, South, North and NULL. How many rows remain after SELECT DISTINCT?
hints: Remove repeated North only.
One NULL remains as a distinct result value.
The remaining values are North, South and NULL; count these result rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: North, South and NULL form three distinct result rows.

questions.prompt: What does DISTINCT change?
hints: SELECT reads; DISTINCT shapes its returned rows.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: DISTINCT removes duplicate selected rows from the query result. It does not delete rows from the stored table.

questions.prompt: What does COUNT(amount) return for the original orders?
hints: Count known values in the column.
COUNT(amount) excludes the NULL row.
Order 106 has no known amount; inspect the amounts on all the other orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five rows have a non-NULL amount; order 106 is missing.

questions.prompt: What is AVG(amount) for the original orders?
hints: Add only known amounts.
Use the count of known amounts as the denominator.
Evaluate 240 ÷ 5; NULL is outside this denominator.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known total is 240 across five known amounts: 240 ÷ 5 = 48.

questions.prompt: What is MIN(amount) for pending orders?
hints: Filter to pending orders first.
Ignore the missing amount; do not replace it with zero.
The pending amounts are a known value on order 104 and NULL on order 106; only the known value participates.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Order 104 is the only pending order with a known amount; MIN is 40.

questions.prompt: With no matching rows, type the value SUM(amount) returns in SQLite.
hints: No observed sum is different from a known zero sum.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: SQLite SUM(amount) returns NULL when there are no non-NULL input values, including an empty matching set. COUNT instead returns zero for an empty set.

questions.prompt: Known values are 10 and 30, with one NULL. What does AVG(value) return?
hints: The missing value does not add to the count.
Divide the known total by two.
Evaluate (10 + 30) ÷ 2; the missing observation is excluded.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: AVG uses the two known values: (10 + 30) ÷ 2 = 20.

questions.prompt: What changes when you use AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0))?
hints: The replacement becomes an input value to AVG.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: COALESCE replaces each missing amount with zero before averaging. Those rows now contribute to the denominator, which can change the average.

questions.prompt: How many result rows does GROUP BY item produce in the original data?
hints: Identify different item names.
One result row represents one item group.
The groups are Book, Desk and Lamp; each gets a result row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are three item groups: Book, Desk and Lamp.

questions.prompt: Within the Lamp group, what is COUNT(amount)?
hints: COUNT(column) counts known values.
Compare the two Lamp amount cells.
In the Lamp group, order 104 has an amount and order 106 has NULL. Count only the known cell.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only order 104 has a known Lamp amount; order 106 is NULL.

questions.prompt: Name the SQL clause that can filter groups on SUM(amount).
hints: The total exists after the rows are grouped.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can test SUM(amount). WHERE filters the input rows before their group totals are computed.

questions.prompt: After WHERE status = 'paid', what is the Desk group's SUM(amount)?
hints: Keep only paid Desk orders.
Add the two eligible amounts.
Evaluate 80 + 80 for the eligible Desk orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Paid Desk orders 101 and 103 have amounts 80 and 80; their total is 160.

questions.prompt: How many item groups survive HAVING SUM(amount) >= 40 in the original data?
hints: Compute each group total first.
The threshold includes totals equal to forty.
The totals are Book 40, Desk 160 and Lamp 40; test each with >= 40.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Book is 40, Desk is 160 and Lamp is 40. All three meet the inclusive threshold.

questions.prompt: What does WHERE status = 'paid' change in a grouped query?
hints: WHERE defines the rows supplied to the groups.

acceptedIdeas: It filters individual rows before grouping
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: WHERE retains only paid input rows before grouping. Group counts and totals are calculated from that filtered set.

choices.label: It filters individual rows before grouping

questions.prompt: How many rows does the correct customers-to-orders INNER JOIN return in the original data?
hints: Count matches, not different names.
Ada, Ben and Cy each contribute two order matches.
Ada, Ben and Cy each have two matches; Dee contributes none to an inner join.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the six orders references one existing customer, so there are six matching pairs.

questions.prompt: Why is Dee absent from the INNER JOIN result?
hints: An inner join requires a match.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An INNER JOIN retains only matching pairs. Dee has no matching order in this dataset, so her customer row contributes no result row.

choices.label: INNER JOIN keeps only the first customer

questions.prompt: How many pairs does CROSS JOIN produce for four customers and six orders?
hints: For each customer, include every order.
Multiply the table sizes.
Evaluate 4 × 6 for every possible customer-order pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every customer pairs with every order: 4 × 6 = 24.

questions.prompt: Which predicate follows the stored relationship?
hints: The order's customer_id refers to the customer's id.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: c.id = o.customer_id follows the customer reference stored on each order. Matching the two tables' unrelated id columns would connect the wrong records.

questions.prompt: Customers A, B and C have two, zero and one orders respectively. How many rows does their INNER JOIN return?
hints: An unmatched customer contributes no inner-join row.
Add the order matches.
Evaluate 2 + 0 + 1; each matching order contributes a row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The matching pairs total 2 + 0 + 1 = 3.

questions.prompt: Why can a customer's name repeat in a correctly joined result?
hints: A one-to-many relationship creates one row for each match.

acceptedIdeas: A person can match several orders
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each matching customer-and-order pair produces a result row. A customer with several orders appears several times without the join being wrong.

choices.label: A person can match several orders
JOIN always duplicates every row twice
Names cannot be selected in SQL

questions.prompt: How many rows does the original customers LEFT JOIN orders return?
hints: Keep each order match.
Add one row for the customer with no match.
Add Dee's preserved unmatched row to the six order matches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six matched order rows plus Dee's unmatched customer row make seven.

questions.prompt: For Dee's group, what does COUNT(o.id) return after the LEFT JOIN?
hints: COUNT(column) ignores NULL.
The retained customer row has a NULL order id.
Dee's order id is NULL; COUNT(o.id) counts only non-NULL matched keys.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Dee has no matched order id, so COUNT(o.id) is zero.

questions.prompt: Where should o.status = 'paid' go if every customer must remain?
hints: Preserve the customer while restricting which orders match.

acceptedIdeas: In ON as a matching condition
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Put the paid condition in ON to limit which orders match while preserving every left-side customer. A WHERE test on the right-side status would remove unmatched customer rows.

choices.label: In ON as a matching condition
In WHERE as the only row filter

questions.prompt: Which predicate identifies customers with no matched order?
hints: An actual order can have a missing amount.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The joined order id is NULL when no order matched. Because stored order ids are non-NULL, o.id IS NULL identifies those unmatched rows.

questions.prompt: How many rows remain with the paid test in ON for the original data?
hints: Count paid matches for each customer.
Retain one row for Dee even without a paid match.
Add Ada's two paid matches, Ben's paid match, Cy's paid match and Dee's preserved row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ada has two paid orders, Ben one and Cy one; Dee remains once with no match. Total: five.

questions.prompt: How many rows pass o.amount IS NULL after the original LEFT JOIN?
hints: A missing amount is not the same as no order.
Inspect both the real missing amount and the unmatched customer.
Inspect order 106's missing amount and the NULL fields in Dee's unmatched row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Cy's order 106 and Dee's unmatched customer row both have NULL amounts.

questions.prompt: customers RIGHT JOIN orders preserves which unmatched row?
hints: RIGHT preserves the right-hand orders table.

acceptedIdeas: Guest order 107, which has no customer reference
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A RIGHT JOIN preserves the orders side. Guest order 107 survives even though it has no matching customer; customer columns for that row are NULL.

choices.label: Guest order 107, which has no customer reference

questions.prompt: How many rows does the FULL OUTER JOIN return with the added guest order?
hints: Keep both kinds of unmatched row.
Do not pair Dee with the guest order; their keys do not match.
Add the six matching pairs and the two unmatched rows from opposite sides.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six matching pairs plus Dee's unmatched row plus the guest order make eight.

questions.prompt: In that full join, c.id IS NULL identifies which case?
hints: Inspect the side named by the missing key.

acceptedIdeas: An order without a matched customer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In the full join, a NULL customer id with an order present marks an order that did not match a customer. The full join preserves unmatched rows from both inputs.

choices.label: An order without a matched customer

questions.prompt: With the paid test in ON, how many unmatched order rows pass c.id IS NULL?
hints: A failed ON test does not remove a preserved order.
Count both pending orders and the guest order.
The unmatched order ids are 104, 106 and 107; count the records rather than their customer references.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Pending orders 104 and 106 do not match under that ON condition; guest order 107 also has no customer match.

questions.prompt: A contains ids 1, 2, 3. B contains ids 2, 4. Each id appears once. How many rows does A FULL JOIN B ON A.id = B.id return?
hints: Count the matching pair once.
Retain all three unmatched ids.
Keep every id from A, then add the id from B that is not already represented.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Id 2 matches; ids 1 and 3 remain from A; id 4 remains from B. Total: four.

questions.prompt: Can two joins have the same row count but retain different records?
hints: LEFT and RIGHT each returned seven here, but their unmatched rows differ.

acceptedIdeas: Yes; compare which side is preserved
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equal row counts do not establish equivalent joins. Inspect the retained records and the NULL-extended columns to see which side each join preserves.

choices.label: Yes; compare which side is preserved
No; equal counts prove equal results
Only when every key is duplicated

questions.prompt: How many orders have amount greater than the original overall AVG(amount)?
hints: Calculate the average of known amounts.
Use a strict greater-than comparison.
The threshold is 240 ÷ 5; test each known amount against it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known average is 48; orders 101 and 103 each have amount 80.

questions.prompt: How many orders belong to North-region customers?
hints: Find customer ids in North first.
Count their orders even when an amount is missing.
North's customer ids are 1 and 3; each contributes two orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Customers 1 and 3 are North; each has two orders.

questions.prompt: Why does EXISTS return Ada once even though she has two orders?
hints: It tests existence without adding each matching subquery row to the outer result.

questions.prompt: How many original orders are strictly above the average for their own item?
hints: Compare within each item group.
Equality does not pass a strict greater-than condition.

questions.prompt: Three customers have zero, one and four orders. How many customers pass EXISTS for an order?
hints: EXISTS asks whether there is at least one match.

Mark each customer whose order count is positive, then count marked customers once.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a subquery that refers to a value from the current outer row?
hints: Its condition depends on which row the outer query is considering.

questions.prompt: How does UNION combine its inputs?
hints: UNION combines results vertically; JOIN matches related rows.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: UNION stacks compatible rows from its SELECT results and removes duplicates. It combines rows vertically rather than matching columns through a join.

choices.label: It matches customer keys to order keys
It changes the stored table names

questions.prompt: How many rows does the paid-id query UNION the at-least-40-id query return?
hints: The two result sets overlap on 101 and 103.
Remove repeated ids from the combined result.
Take four paid ids and three large ids, then remove the two repeated ids.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The unique ids are 101, 102, 103, 104 and 105.

questions.prompt: How many rows result when UNION also selects the different labels 'paid' and 'large'?

courseChecks.description: Trace repair records through a query. Use the result to choose where to begin.

visual.sql: SELECT id FROM repairs WHERE tech = 1;

question.prompt: Each row is one repair. How many repairs refer to technician 1?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Repairs 11 and 12 refer to technician 1. Repeating a technician key is compatible with one repair per row.

visual.sql:
SELECT fee + 8 AS quoted
FROM repairs WHERE id = 11;

question.prompt: The workshop adds a fixed 8 to each known fee. What is quoted for repair 11?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The selected fee is 30, so the quoted value is 30 + 8 = 38. The alias names the output column.

visual.sql:
SELECT id FROM repairs
WHERE status = 'done' AND fee BETWEEN 30 AND 60;

question.prompt: How many repairs meet this condition, including both fee boundaries?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Repairs 11, 12 and 14 are done and have fees in the inclusive interval 30 to 60.

question.prompt: Which repair id appears first after this ordering?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Repairs 12 and 14 tie at 60. The ascending id tie-breaker puts 12 first.

visual.sql: SELECT DISTINCT tech FROM repairs;

question.prompt: How many distinct technician entries are returned, counting a returned NULL entry?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The distinct entries are 1, 2 and NULL. DISTINCT retains one NULL entry.

visual.sql: SELECT AVG(fee) FROM repairs;

question.prompt: What average fee does this query return?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four known fees sum to 165. AVG skips the missing fee, so 165 / 4 = 41.25.

visual.sql:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS jobs
FROM repairs GROUP BY status HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

question.prompt: How many status groups survive this HAVING condition?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The done group has three rows and the open group has two. Only done survives.

visual.sql:
SELECT t.name, r.id FROM techs AS t
JOIN repairs AS r ON r.tech = t.id;

question.prompt: How many matching repair rows does this inner join return?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Technicians 1 and 2 each match two repairs. The unassigned repair and technician 3 produce no inner-join row.

question.prompt: What job count does the left join report for Uma?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Uma is preserved in the left join, but her right-side repair id is NULL. COUNT(r.id) is zero.

SELECT t.name, r.id FROM techs AS t
FULL OUTER JOIN repairs AS r ON r.tech = t.id;

question.prompt: How many rows does this full outer join return?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are four matching pairs, Uma's unmatched row and repair 15's unmatched row: six rows.

question.prompt: How many technicians have at least one done repair?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ira and Sol each have a done repair. EXISTS returns each qualifying outer technician once.

question.prompt: How many ids remain after UNION removes repeats?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first set contains 11, 12 and 14; the second contains 12 and 14. Their union has three ids.

visual.sql:
SELECT id, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY fee DESC) AS place
FROM repairs WHERE fee IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

question.prompt: What rank does repair 11 receive when fees alone define ties?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two fees of 60 share rank 1. The next fee, 30, receives rank 3.

question.prompt: What position is assigned to repair 14 inside its technician's partition?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Technician 2 has repairs 13 and 14, so repair 14 is second in that partition.

visual.sql:
SELECT id, LAG(fee) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS previous_fee
FROM repairs ORDER BY id;

question.prompt: What previous fee is attached to repair 14?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The previous repair is 13, whose fee is missing. LAG reads that missing value rather than skipping to repair 12.

courseChecks.title: Bring it together
courseChecks.description: Audit a new field-sampling report across filters, joins, summaries and windows.

visual.sql: SELECT id, reading FROM samples WHERE id = 22;

question.prompt: A sample id identifies one collected sample. Does the missing reading make sample 22 disappear from this result?

acceptedIdeas: The row remains with an unknown reading
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sample 22 still exists. Its reading is unknown, so the returned row has id 22 and a NULL reading.

choices.label: The row remains with an unknown reading

visual.sql: SELECT reading * 2 AS adjusted FROM samples WHERE id = 22;

question.prompt: Which value is returned in adjusted for sample 22?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Multiplication involving NULL produces NULL. Renaming the result does not supply a missing measurement.

visual.sql: SELECT id FROM samples WHERE site = 'A' OR reading IS NULL;

question.prompt: How many samples are from site A or have an unknown reading?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Samples 21 and 22 meet at least one condition. Sample 22 meeting both does not duplicate the row.

visual.sql:
SELECT id FROM samples WHERE reading IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY reading ASC, id DESC LIMIT 1;

question.prompt: The lowest known reading is wanted. Which id does this query return?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The smallest known reading is 2, from sample 25. The missing value is excluded before sorting.

visual.sql: SELECT DISTINCT site, reading FROM samples;

question.prompt: How many distinct site-and-reading pairs remain?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Samples 23 and 24 repeat the same pair (B, 10). All other pairs differ, including the two A pairs.

visual.sql: SELECT AVG(COALESCE(reading, 0)) FROM samples;

question.prompt: Which calculation gives the average when each unknown reading is explicitly filled with zero?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The chosen policy makes six values: 4, 0, 10, 10, 2 and 6. Their sum is 32, so the mean is 32 / 6.

question.prompt: How many site groups have at least two known readings after the row filter?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The row filter retains 21, 23, 24 and 26. Only site B contributes two of those known readings.

visual.sql:
SELECT s.code, m.id FROM sites AS s
JOIN samples AS m ON m.site = s.code;

question.prompt: How many sample rows survive a join to the listed sites?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A matches samples 21 and 22; B matches 23 and 24. C and the unknown site have no listed match.

visual.sql:
SELECT s.code, COUNT(m.id) AS n FROM sites AS s
LEFT JOIN samples AS m
  ON m.site = s.code AND m.reading >= 8
GROUP BY s.code ORDER BY s.code;

question.prompt: The query keeps sites even without a reading of at least 8. Which site appears first?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A and D each have zero qualifying samples. The first ordered row is A; the condition in ON preserves it.

visual.sql:
SELECT s.code, m.id FROM sites AS s
RIGHT JOIN samples AS m ON m.site = s.code;

question.prompt: How many input samples does this right join preserve?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All six samples survive because samples is the right table. C and the unknown site receive NULL site-table fields.

visual.sql:
SELECT id FROM samples
WHERE reading > (SELECT AVG(reading) FROM samples);

question.prompt: How many samples exceed the average of the known readings?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known mean is 32 / 5 = 6.4. Only samples 23 and 24, each with reading 10, exceed it.

question.prompt: How many rows are retained when both reports are concatenated?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first report has ids 21 and 22; the second has id 22. UNION ALL retains both copies of 22.

visual.sql:
SELECT id, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY reading DESC) AS place
FROM samples WHERE reading IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

question.prompt: What dense rank is assigned to the reading of sample 26?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The distinct readings descend as 10, 6, 4 and 2. Reading 6 receives dense rank 2 despite the two top rows.

question.prompt: How many rows are kept when the first sample per recorded site is selected?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The recorded sites A, B and C each contribute their first sample. The unknown site is filtered before partitioning.

question.prompt: What running total appears for sample 23 when the frame includes all rows from its day?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: By day 2, the frame contains readings 4, NULL, 10 and 10. SUM skips NULL and returns 24 for both day-2 samples.

question.prompt: A row represents one delivery, with id as its identifier. How many delivery rows have no assigned hub?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Delivery 36 has no assigned hub. Delivery 35 has a recorded hub X even though X is absent from the hub lookup.

visual.sql:
SELECT id AS delivery, weight * 1000 AS grams
FROM deliveries WHERE id = 31;

question.prompt: How many columns are in this report?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The SELECT list contains two expressions. Their aliases are delivery and grams; the stored table is unchanged.

visual.sql:
SELECT id FROM deliveries
WHERE status = 'sent' AND (hub = 'N' OR hub = 'S');

question.prompt: How many rows satisfy the intended sent-and-chosen-hub condition?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Deliveries 31, 32 and 34 are sent and belong to N or S. The parentheses keep the sent requirement on both hubs.

visual.sql:
SELECT id FROM deliveries WHERE status = 'sent'
ORDER BY day DESC, id ASC LIMIT 1;

question.prompt: Which delivery wins the latest-day ordering after the sent filter?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sent rows occur on days 1, 2, 3 and 4. Delivery 36 is the latest.

visual.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT hub) FROM deliveries;

question.prompt: How many known distinct hub codes does COUNT(DISTINCT hub) count?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: N, S and X are the three known codes. COUNT(DISTINCT hub) excludes the NULL entry.

visual.sql: SELECT SUM(weight) FROM deliveries WHERE status = 'cancelled';

question.prompt: What does SUM return when no delivery matches the filter?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With no matching input rows, SUM returns NULL. COUNT(*) would return zero for the same input.

question.prompt: Which recorded hub has a sent-weight total above 10?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: N has sent weights 12 and 8, totaling 20. S has only 3 after the sent filter.

visual.sql:
SELECT d.id, r.route FROM dispatch AS d
JOIN routes AS r ON r.hub = d.hub;

question.prompt: A route lookup has duplicate hub keys. How many joined rows does the query produce?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the two dispatch rows matches each of the three N routes. The join produces 2 × 3 = 6 rows.

question.prompt: How many hubs does a WHERE filter on the right-hand status leave?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: N and S have sent matches. W's NULL-extended row fails the WHERE condition, so W disappears.

question.prompt: How many unmatched rows appear as well as the four matching pairs?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Hub W is unmatched on the left. Deliveries 35 and 36 are unmatched on the right. That makes three unmatched rows.

question.prompt: Which hub has no delivery rows at all?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: N and S each have deliveries. No delivery has hub W, so only W passes NOT EXISTS.

visual.sql:
SELECT hub, 'sent' AS source FROM deliveries
WHERE status = 'sent' AND hub IS NOT NULL
UNION
SELECT hub, 'held' AS source FROM deliveries
WHERE status = 'held';

question.prompt: The source label is part of each selected row. How many rows survive UNION?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The distinct full rows are (N, sent), (S, sent), (S, held) and (X, held). The two S rows have different source labels.

visual.sql:
SELECT id, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY weight DESC, id ASC) AS place
FROM deliveries WHERE weight IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

question.prompt: What rank does delivery 33 receive when id is also inside the window ordering?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The weight-12 rows have ids 31 and 33, so they no longer tie across the complete window ordering. Delivery 33 has rank 2.

visual.sql:
SELECT id, SUM(weight) OVER (PARTITION BY hub) AS hub_weight
FROM deliveries ORDER BY id;

question.prompt: What N-partition total is repeated beside delivery 32?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two N deliveries weigh 12 and 8. The window adds 20 beside each without collapsing their rows.

visual.sql:
SELECT id, LEAD(weight) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_weight
FROM deliveries ORDER BY id;

question.prompt: What is the next delivery's weight after delivery 34 in id order?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Delivery 35 is next, and its weight is missing. LEAD returns that NULL rather than delivery 36's weight.
